conbody.p: Impala can authenticate hs2-http client connections using OAuth 2.0 bearer access tokens. With this form of authentication, a client presents a signed token in the Authorization HTTP header of each request. Impala verifies the token's signature against one or more configured identity provider(s), optionally validates the token's aud (audience) and iss (issuer) claims, and then determines identity of the connecting user from a configurable claim in the token.
conbody.note: Impala's OAuth support only accepts access tokens that are structured and signed as JSON Web Tokens (JWTs). Impala verifies the token locally using a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS); it does not support opaque OAuth access tokens that must be validated by calling an authorization server's token-introspection endpoint. Confirm that your identity provider issues JWT-structured access tokens before configuring OAuth authentication for Impala.
conbody.p: Alternative forms of authentication you can use instead of, or alongside, OAuth are Kerberos, described in , and LDAP, described in .

Only client-to-Impala connections can be authenticated using OAuth tokens, and only over the HTTP-based transport, that is, connections made over the HiveServer2 HTTP endpoint (--hs2_http_port) and the Impala coordinator debug web UI (--webserver_port). OAuth authentication is not supported on the executor debug web UI.
When a request arrives with an Authorization: Bearer token header, Impala:

ol.li: Decodes the token and reads its header to determine which key ID and signing algorithm were used.

Looks through its list of configured identity providers for the first one whose keys could have produced the token, and attempts to verify the token's signature using that provider's keys. If verification fails, Impala continues checking any remaining providers that could also have produced the token.

If the token's signature is verified, and the provider is configured with audienceClaims or issuerClaims, checks that the token's aud and/or iss claims match one of the configured values. If the claims do not match, Impala continues by checking any remaining providers that could also have produced the token.
Extracts the connecting user's name from the claim named by the provider's usernameClaim (username, by default).

conbody.p: For hs2-http client connections, after a token has been successfully verified, Impala returns a session cookie to the client so that subsequent requests in the same session do not need to re-verify the token. Connections to the debug Web UIs must provide the token with each request.

Because the bearer token is equivalent to a password for the lifetime of the token, OAuth authentication must only be used over an encrypted connection. By default, impalad refuses to start with --oauth_token_auth=true unless TLS is configured for client connections. For more information about configuring TLS, see .
Start impalad with the following flag to turn on bearer-token authentication.

dd.p: When true, Impala reads the OAuth token out of the HTTP Authorization header and extracts the username from the token payload.

conbody.note: The --jwt_token_auth, --jwks_file_path, --jwks_url, --jwks_verify_server_certificate, --jwks_ca_certificate, --jwks_update_frequency_s, --jwks_pulling_timeout_s, --jwt_custom_claim_username, --jwt_allow_without_tls, --oauth_jwks_file_path, --oauth_jwks_url, --oauth_jwks_verify_server_certificate, --oauth_jwks_ca_certificate, --oauth_jwks_update_frequency_s, --oauth_jwks_pulling_timeout_s, and --oauth_jwt_custom_claim_username, flags are deprecated and should not be used. If set, the flags will still be recognized, but migration to the new flags is recommended.
conbody.p: Use the --oauth_servers startup flag to configure Impala with identity provider(s) to trust. Its value is a JSON array, with one JSON object per identity provider. Configuring more than one entry allows Impala to accept tokens issued by more than one identity provider.
Each entry in the array supports the following fields. Only jwksFilePath or jwksUrl is required; all other fields are optional.

dd.p: File path of a pre-installed JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) file, in the local filesystem of every host running impalad, used to verify tokens issued by this provider. Mutually exclusive with jwksUrl.
URL from which Impala downloads the JWKS used to verify tokens issued by this provider. Mutually exclusive with jwksFilePath.
File path of a PEM bundle of root CA certificates to trust when downloading the JWKS from jwksUrl. Only applicable when jwksUrl is set.
Whether the TLS certificate presented by the jwksUrl server is verified when downloading the JWKS. The default value is true. Only applicable when jwksUrl is set.
dd.note: Do not set to false outside of dev/test environments.

dd.p: Number of seconds to wait for the connection to jwksUrl to time out when downloading the JWKS. The default value is 10. Only applicable when jwksUrl is set.

Number of seconds to wait between re-downloading the JWKS from jwksUrl, so that key rotation on the identity provider side is picked up without restarting Impala. The default value is 60. Only applicable when jwksUrl is set.
Name of the claim in the token payload that holds the Impala username to authenticate as, for example username or sub. The default value is username.

Array of acceptable values for the token's aud claim. If specified and non-empty, a token from this provider is only accepted if its aud claim matches one of the listed values. If omitted or empty, the aud claim is not checked.

Array of acceptable values for the token's iss claim. If specified and non-empty, a token from this provider is only accepted if its iss claim matches one of the listed values. If omitted or empty, the iss claim is not checked.

conbody.p: For example, the following value for --oauth_servers configures two identity providers: one whose JWKS is downloaded from a URL and whose tokens must have been issued for the impala-service audience by the auth_iss issuer, and a second, simpler provider whose JWKS is read from a local file.
conbody.note: Pass the JSON value as a single shell argument, for example by surrounding it with single quotes, so that the double quotes and braces are not interpreted by the shell.
conbody.p: The --oauth_servers flag only declares identity providers that Impala can use for token verification. You must still set --oauth_token_auth=true to actually check for a bearer token on incoming connections.

concept.title: Combining OAuth with other authentication methods

conbody.p: OAuth authentication can be enabled at the same time as LDAP, Kerberos SPNEGO, or SAML authentication for the same impalad. Impala inspects each incoming HTTP request and determines which mechanism to use for it as follows: an existing session cookie is tried first; otherwise, if the Authorization header is a Bearer token that looks like a JWT (it contains at least one . character), Impala attempts OAuth verification before falling back to any other configured mechanism, such as SAML, LDAP, or SPNEGO.
Each impalad exposes metrics that count the number of successful and failed bearer-token authentication attempts, both for the HiveServer2 HTTP endpoint and for the debug web UI:

These metrics only count the initial token verification for a connection. Subsequent requests on the same connection that are authenticated using the session cookie Impala issues after a successful token verification instead increment the related total-cookie-auth-success metrics.
conbody.note: Since session cookies are issued only for hs2-http client connections, the webserver metrics will increment with each request.
conbody.p: When token verification fails, Impala returns an HTTP 401 response with a WWW-Authenticate header describing the reason for the failure, for example an expired token or a token signed by a key that does not match any configured identity provider.
